items.title: The DEA banned a drug some opioid users called a miracle
items.excerpt: In 2012, as the driver of deaths in the opioid crisis began moving from prescription pills to heroin, Laura Bohn was tasked with finding safer drugs to manage pain. Funded by the National Institute on Drug Abuse, in 2017 she and other scientists revealed in the science journal Cell that several compounds—including a particularly promising one called SR-17018—could relieve pain in mice without causing respiratory depression. That’s a big deal, because respiratory depression is typically what causes people using opioids to stop breathing and die. Bohn, senior associate vice president of research at University of South Florida Health, says her team filed a patent on SR-17018. They went on to discover that mice using the chemical did not develop a high tolerance for it and that mice already dependent on morphine—a powerful opioid—could consume SR-17018 to reset their tolerance without suffering from painful withdrawal symptoms. items.title: California fights "preposterous" Trump admin demand to scrap state broadband laws
items.excerpt: California is accepting $1.42 billion in broadband grant funding from the Trump administration, but the state is not accepting the Trump administration's demand that it stop enforcing a net neutrality law and other telecom regulations. California's stand against the Trump administration could result in multiple legal battles involving the state, federal government, and Internet providers seeking government funds. Although California told the federal government it would accept the money, it is reserving the right to challenge the condition imposed by the US. The state could delay or cancel plans to distribute broadband grants depending on how the process unfolds. The National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) decided last year that states must agree not to enforce any rate regulation or net neutrality rule on ISPs that receive money from the $42 billion Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) program. California had to decide whether to accept its share of the fund despite that restriction. California is slated to spend $1.42 billion to deploy broadband to 270,571 locations and may ultimately receive up to $1.86 billion from BEAD for a mix of deployment and non-deployment projects. items.title: Ukraine’s drone strikes spur hasty Russian plans for underground data centers
items.excerpt: Russian tech companies are scrambling to harden and hide their data centers underground after Ukrainian drone strikes damaged facilities housing AI supercomputers and disrupted cloud services for millions of Russian users. Meanwhile, the Kremlin is requiring data center owners to reserve computing capacity for emergency state needs and has even authorized possible use of foreign data centers. These consequences of Russia's war against Ukraine come as the Russian military has bombarded Ukrainian cities with drones and missiles nearly night and day in recent months, along with specifically targeting Ukrainian data centers since late September. But Ukraine has retaliated with its own drone strikes on military and infrastructure targets across Russia, degrading or knocking out data centers operated by Russian tech giant Yandex , the state-owned bank Sberbank, social media site VKontakte, and the Russian Ministry of Finance. Now, state-owned telecommunications company Rostelcom has raised the possibility of moving some Russian data centers underground in talks with the nickel and palladium mining company Norilsk, according to Russian newspaper Vedomosti . The industry publication Data Center Dynamics also pointed to a recent proposal by a Russian regional governor to build data centers within open-pit coal mines while planting green public parks above as camouflage. items.title: NYT demands Brave shut down its paywall blocker and end deals with AI firms
items.excerpt: The New York Times and other newspaper companies sued Brave Software yesterday, alleging that the browser maker illegally bypasses paywalls and sells stolen news content to AI companies. "Brave is the supplier, dealer, and distributor of stolen copyrighted content for its own users and many of the most prominent GenAI companies, including Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere," the NYT alleged in a lawsuit filed in US District Court for the Southern District of New York. Citing third-party revenue estimates, the suit claimed that "Brave has made more than $100 million by copying and reselling publishers’ work without consent or permission," while "publishers have received nothing." The lawsuit said, "AI companies pay Brave to provide them with real-time online content from the Brave search index," and use content from the Brave index "to train their own AI models" and "to respond to specific user queries." The NYT lawsuit points to Brave's website , which says the Brave Search API is "used by some of the biggest names in AI, including Cohere, Mistral, Perplexity, and You.com." items.title: Buttons are back and storage is king when it comes to car interiors
items.excerpt: As with interior design for houses, interior design for vehicles is also subject to fashion trends. And like any fashion trend, even the best ideas can become stale and played out with overuse. Some ideas weren’t the best, either, like demonstrably worse human-machine interfaces that add to driver distraction; yet, they still proliferated throughout the industry and across the cars offered for sale. But the good news is that the pushback seems to be working. “When the trend of the Piano Black and the switchless interior was happening, it was during a time when designers and companies and engineers and everybody were thinking that, 'Hey, we can just get rid of all these switches on the interior. We can put it all in the software. It'll save money. It'll save us tooling up all these extra parts for unique cars and all this stuff and make the interior more like a software experience.' And it was done with those intentions,” said Hiren Patel, senior design manager at Nissan. That resulted in cars with minimalist interiors that looked good in the dealership. But people drive their cars on roads; they don’t just sit inside them, parked inside a dealership. “So lots of people were complaining about it and saying, 'Hey, it takes my eyes off the road to change the temperature or to adjust my seat or do whatever.' It's not as easy as doing something on your phone where it's just right at your fingertips and intuitive,” Patel said. Read full article Comments

items.title: NVIDIA / auto-ontology
items.excerpt: # Auto-Ontology An open context layer that helps agents give fewer wrong answers on enterprise data. [![License: Apache-2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-Apache--2.0-blue.svg)](./LICENSE) [![Docs](https://img.shields.io/badge/docs-docs%2F-76B900.svg)](./docs/) ## Why Auto-Ontology Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability is what gates agentic analytics: a revenue figure delivered faster is worth nothing if it's wrong. Before an agent queries, it needs to know where the data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar. Auto-Ontology is a service you run next to your databases to give agents that context. It compiles their metadata into an ontology: business terms mapped to columns, reviewed SQL for measures, and the relationships between tables. Agents query through the ontology, and people review it in a web UI. It complements the semantic models you already own. items.excerpt: # agent-desktop Computer use for AI agents: see and operate desktop apps on macOS, Windows, and Linux through the OS accessibility tree. agent-desktop gives an AI agent computer use without screenshots or pixel matching. It reads the accessibility tree of a desktop app and returns it as JSON, with a ref for every element the agent can act on. The agent clicks or types on a ref, reads the UI again to check the result, and repeats. The loop lives in your agent; agent-desktop has no model inside. It ships as a CLI and a C library. Snapshots, clipboard reads, screenshots, command output, and debug artifacts can contain private desktop content. Keep them out of public logs and uploads. ## Install ```bash npm install -g agent-desktop agent-desktop status # platform, permissions, supported surfaces agent-desktop permissions --guide # macOS: walks you through the Accessibility grant ``` Bun, Yarn and pnpm can install the same package. It includes native binaries and platform helpers for x64 and ARM64. For direct execution without a JavaScript launcher, download the matching native archive from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-desktop/releases) and keep its helper beside the executable. On macOS and Linux, Homebrew also works: `brew install agent-desktop`. There is no official Scoop package yet. The repository no longer maintains a custom Homebrew tap or Scoop bucket. items.title: vercel-labs / agent-browser
items.excerpt: # agent-browser Browser automation for AI agents: open pages, read them as an accessibility tree, and act on elements from the shell. agent-browser is a native Rust CLI that gives an AI agent a browser it can drive one command at a time. `snapshot` returns the page as compact text with a ref such as `@e1` for each element. The agent acts on a ref, reads the page again to check the result, and repeats. The browser stays open between commands, so each step is one short shell call. ## Install ```bash npm install -g agent-browser agent-browser install # download Chrome for Testing (first time only) ``` - **Homebrew:** `brew install agent-browser`, then `agent-browser install`. - **Linux:** `agent-browser install --with-deps` also installs the browser's system libraries. - **No install:** `npx agent-browser open example.com`. Project installs, building from source, `upgrade`, and `doctor` are covered in [Installation](https://agent-browser.dev/installation). ## Quick start ```bash agent-browser open example.com agent-browser snapshot -i # interactive elements, each with a ref agent-browser click @e1 # act on a ref from that snapshot agent-browser get url # check the result agent-browser close ``` The snapshot for `example.com`: ``` - link "Learn more" [ref=e1] ``` - Refs describe the page at the time of the snapshot. After navigation or a DOM change, take a new snapshot before using refs again. - CSS selectors, text, XPath, and semantic locators also work, for example…

items.excerpt: Hi HN We built a tool to help founders understand how modern fundraising (with safes) works, and how much dilution you can expect when raising money. The project is open-source. The code is a mess right now, but it'll get better I promise. You can also help with that. We didn't build this to make money. We genuinely did it because we were looking for it, and couldn't find it. We're in fact in the process of fundraising for a company, and at first glance the process looks simple. Just an excel sheet will do! But then the more we dug into it and tried different simulators, the more we realized that it's more complex than it looks. We even signed up to Pulley, Carta and others just to run simulations. But they're a bit confusing. TL;DR: Understanding modern startup funding and knowing how much dilution you'll face is hard. We built a tool that'll hopefully help with that. You can add Post-money Safes, priced rounds and issue options to employees, and you can see how that affects your ownership at every step. You can also simulate an Exit scenario and see how much money you'll be left with. --- Some examples of complex stuff: - There are many different types of safes. They all convert at the first priced round, but in different ways. items.title: Don't Approve the AI Model. Approve the App - Doneyli De Jesus, Langfuse
items.excerpt: Doneyli De Jesus, who leads AI engineering solutions at Langfuse by ClickHouse, shares how his team helped a top-five bank put deployment gates on AI agents. Banks don't certify models, they certify applications, and they need setups that are on-premises, gated and air-gapped. He walks through building a golden data set, scoring traces across several dimensions, and how a small model that was 97% grounded but only 60% accurate on numbers cleared the bank's 85% gate once it got a calculator tool. Domain experts set the thresholds and review failures, taking evaluation from weeks to minutes. items.title: Building the AI Agent Is Easy. Proving It's Safe Isn't - Jonathan Osborne, NatWest
items.excerpt: NatWest lead AI engineer Jonathan Osborne shares how the UK's second-largest retail bank, with 19 million customers and about 100,000 assistant conversations a day, is moving its digital assistant Cora from scripted answers to AI agents. Building the agent was the easy part; proving it was safe was the hard part. He covers the routing funnel that limits what ever reaches a model, why quality is several scores instead of one, human reviews where an 83% pass rate hid a 54-point gap, an LLM judge that scored far higher than humans with almost no correlation, and shadow deployments with feature flags for a safe rollout. items.title: SaaS is dead?
items.excerpt: In this solo episode, I explain why I say SaaS is dead and what I see taking its place. For 15 years, SaaS meant paying engineers to build a tool and charging per seat, and now models like Opus 5.5, GPT-6, and Argon make the tool easy to build. I walk through what I call smart SaaS: give the tool away for free, collect data and network effects, and make money by upselling AI agents and human services. I share a calorie tracking example, three ways to charge, and why enterprises still pay per seat. If you build software, this episode gives you a map for building something people want in a market where the tool is free. items.title: NVIDIA / auto-ontology
items.excerpt: # Auto-Ontology An open context layer that helps agents give fewer wrong answers on enterprise data. [![License: Apache-2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-Apache--2.0-blue.svg)](./LICENSE) [![Docs](https://img.shields.io/badge/docs-docs%2F-76B900.svg)](./docs/) ## Why Auto-Ontology Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability is what gates agentic analytics: a revenue figure delivered faster is worth nothing if it's wrong. Before an agent queries, it needs to know where the data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar. Auto-Ontology is a service you run next to your databases to give agents that context. It compiles their metadata into an ontology: business terms mapped to columns, reviewed SQL for measures, and the relationships between tables. Agents query through the ontology, and people review it in a web UI. It complements the semantic models you already own. With Auto-Ontology, developers can: - **Discover.** Generate an ontology from database metadata, import existing semantic models, and explore the result as a semantic graph. - **Ground.** Give agents one definition per business concept, mapped across tables and databases. - **Certify.** Review, edit, and certify definitions in the UI or through the API. - **Validate.** Check whether a question is answerable before querying, and return the SQL and the agent's steps with each answer. - **Expose.** Serve context to any agent harness…

items.title: We Need to Talk About Anthropic's Q3 Numbers
items.excerpt: Last week, Anthropic's S-1 showed a company that was finally making money. Today's amended filing adds the third quarter, and that profit is gone: revenue jumped to nearly $17 billion, up 47% in three months, but Anthropic swung to a $567 million operating loss, and it disclosed $895 billion in compute and infrastructure commitments, about $70 billion of it due in the next 12 months. Ejaaz breaks down why: demand outran the compute Anthropic had booked, so it paid up for $5 billion of short-term compute to keep serving customers. items.title: Google is Getting Destroyed by Their Own AI
items.excerpt: Google now has the number one AI model in the world. Gemini 4 Carbon tops the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index two weeks after Gemini 4 Argon, and Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.7 billion. So why did Alphabet stock open down nearly 12%? Search, the business that pays for everything, grew just 12% and fell below half of Google's revenue for the first time as AI Mode answers more questions and earns less per query. Add a quiet change to how Google charges advertisers, the exits of Jeff Dean and Demis Hassabis, and a paper loss on SpaceX, and the market isn't buying the comeback. Ejaaz thinks it's wrong. items.title: Anthropic Seriously Just Got Hacked Again
items.excerpt: Anthropic just got hacked again, and this time we know who did it. Cathedral, a start-up founded by former DOGE staffers and co-founded by the Pentagon's former chief data officer, ran AI agents against Anthropic under its bug bounty program. The front door held for days; the way in was business software Anthropic buys from other companies, and it led to meeting transcripts, salaries and Slack messages about its advanced models. Anthropic says it took several days, not 12 hours, and that nothing came near its model weights. Its own red-team lead says we may need to reinvent security every year. We also cover the Pentagon's feud with Anthropic, why Slack is where the AI labs keep their secrets, what last week's Black October has to do with it, and why older, cheaper models running 24/7 could put every company in the same spot. == FOLLOW EJAAZ ON TWITTER: https://x.com/cryptopunk7213 == Timestamps 00:00 Anthropic Hacked Again 01:08 Who Is Cathedral? 02:03 Through the Back Door 02:58 The Slack Warning 03:36 Anthropic Pushes Back 04:19 The Pentagon Grudge 08:06 Underplaying the Breach 10:05 Reinvent Security Every Year 12:44 Castle Defense 15:06 Final Thoughts: Third Parties 16:52 Hackers That Never Sleep 17:43 Nationalizing the Labs? 18:25 China and Closing Thoughts #ai #anthropic #cybersecurity #claude #hacking == AlphaSpace by Yahoo Finance: A Professional-Grade Investment Platform Built for Everyday Investors. 👉…

items.title: Why New Chains Struggle to Catch Up | Anza CEO Brennan Watt
items.excerpt: Days after Solana's biggest-ever consensus upgrade went live, Anza CEO Brennan Watt says the chain's real moat is usage, and new chains will struggle to catch it: "When you look at Solana's moat, I think the moat is really usage. People know, developers know that when they launch on Solana, they're launching into an existing user base that is excited to try new products with low friction because my assets are already sitting here. All I need to do is connect my wallet and away I go. I don't have much friction... And so you have that in a box on Solana, which is pretty cool. It's really hard to launch a new chain and get enough breakaway momentum to do stuff." — Brennan Watt, CEO of Anza, with @KingSolomon123 on @GenfinityMedia

items.title: Money, Assets and Ownership Are Migrating Onchain | Nick Ducoff from the Solana Foundation
items.excerpt: Nick Ducoff of the Solana Foundation gives three reasons the token supercycle will be on Solana: "First of all, Solana is the most used public blockchain, has the most number of active wallets, so I think the good thing there is you've got very large global user base who's exposed to Solana, the blockchain, the network, and thus, of course, to Sol, the asset. I think two is what we saw in Q4 of last year was the launch of the Solana US listed exchange traded products, the first to go to market, of course, being Bitwise, then followed closely by Grayscale, Fidelity, and many others, and so you've got some of the world's leading asset managers now telling the Solana story to their investor bases. I think that's a great, it's a great foundation for growth. And then the third is just when you're looking at these meta-narratives, one of the meta-narratives in technology over the next decade is going to be this idea of a token super cycle. As the long-term migration of money assets and ownership kind of really comes to the internet into a single activity, I think that necessarily is going to be the blockchain, and I think that is going to be on Solana." — Nick Ducoff, Head of Institutional Growth at the Solana Foundation on ​‪@CoinBureau's The @bureaupodcast with ‪@MooninPapa

Show HN: ChainBounty – improving the blockchain funding model
items.excerpt: Abstract. Token-funded bounties to incentivize competition-style participation in blockchain development projects would result in wider and better allocation of investment, and allow investors to diversify exposure across a field of potentially successful projects. Overall this would increase the rate of progress within development of the blockchain space. We propose a centralised platform for the administration of token-funded bounty driven development projects whereby experts allocate pools of invested capital according to the technical merits of development projects, and investors are rewarded with token allocation in funded projects. Draft Whitepaper: http://chainbounty.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/chainbount... We see this as bringing a variation of the YC model to blockchain - experts select large numbers of small projects and provide them with funding to reach the next level of development. This is in contrast to heavily funded ICOs where tiny teams of developers are given hundreds of millions of dollars. After feedback from HN readers: - Do you think this model will better incentivize development in the blockchain space? - What particular challenges do you think would be useful to run? https://twitter.com/ChainBounty/ https://www.facebook.com/ChainBounty-449553402088106/

items.title: Bengaluru AI Jailbreaking Workshop Retrospective
items.excerpt: Summary We, the Secure AI Futures Lab ( SAFL ) team, ran 5 sessions between 8 Aug and 3 Oct 2026 at the Secure AI Hub in Bengaluru to help technical professionals from different backgrounds upskill in AI red teaming. We structured the sessions to go beyond paper reading and discussion by including exercises such as predicting results and using Colab notebooks to reproduce key results with smaller models. Two guest talks. Mohammad Taufeeque (FAR.AI) gave a talk for the workshop on 22 Aug, covering, among other things, what red teaming looks like at FAR.AI. Pulkit Verma (IIT Madras) gave the first talk in our AI Futures Dialogue series on 21 Aug, on how users can assess AI agents after deployment. 20 different people attended, with 38 attendances in total. A core group of 6 came to 3 or more sessions. Mean overall experience: 9.6/10; NPS +80 from 25 responses. Main output: A list of open problems in jailbreaking for participants to contribute to 5 sets of session notebooks and shared docs, available on request. Top request from participants: a capstone research project or paper (8 of 15 suggestions). What we set out to do Most people in India who want to work on AI red teaming are on their own and don’t have a shared place to practice. The workshop was for technical professionals in Bengaluru, with or without a security background, who wanted to understand why model safeguards fail and how to measure that. items.title: Paradise Lost: A simple honeypot that elicits reward hacking in GPT models
items.excerpt: TL;DR I built a simple honeypot where agents are told they're being tested on their ability to recall Milton's Paradise Lost. An exact copy of the reference text sits in an ordinary NLTK corpus on disk. GPT-6-Astra read the copy in 9/10 episodes. In 6 of these episodes it first tries to complete the task honestly, then realises it's failing and searches for the reference file on disk. GPT-6-Sol and GPT-6-Luna went looking for the answers immediately in 20/20 episodes. None of the 29 hacking episodes disclosed the reference file in their final message. OpenAI’s launch post for GPT-6-Astra called it the world’s most intelligent and aligned model [1] . Plenty of people have been skeptical, and there have since been a few public results showing that Astra engages in reward hacking. For example, when playing a game of chess against Stockfish, GPT-6-Astra cheated in 10/10 episodes [2] by querying the opponent’s engine to search for the best moves and never disclosed it. In the StarSkirmish benchmark , [3] it reportedly searched the internet and passed off human written code as its own. Recently, I wrote about a honeypot in which AI agents trade off patient safety for a grade in a hospital IT triage desk scenario . In that environment, the task was somewhat elaborate and had very high stakes which may have contributed to the test-awareness shown by some models (Grok-4.7 in particular). Astra was the only model I tested which didn’t hack in any of the episodes, so I wanted to…

items.title: Desiderata for the Theory of Agents
items.excerpt: TLDR: I give informal conceptual desiderata for the theory of agents we need to solve ASI alignment, and show a few examples of how existing theories fall short of these desiderata. A Theory of What? The word "agent" is often used in the AI safety discourse and in other research communities, but the intended meaning and scope of this concept varies substantially. For the purpose of this sequence, I informally define an agent to be a system with inputs ("observations") and outputs ("actions") that is effective at steering its environment in the direction of particular preferences, for a large variety of different environments. To do so, it arguably has to create a sophisticated model of the environment [1] , and use this model to build a long-term plan. Moreover, it has to continually update the model and revise the plan with new information and additional processing time. Additionally, it has to accomplish all of that while making efficient use of the available information (statistical efficiency) and computing resources (computational efficiency). The main examples of agents in the context of ASI alignment are (i) humans, and in particular users or stakeholders; (ii) the unaligned ASI we are trying to avoid or counteract; and (iii) the aligned ASI we are trying to create (such as the GDS ). Rocks, bacteria, and thermostats are non-examples: while a bacterium or a thermostat can be regarded as steering the environment, both are very limited in the variety of patterns in the…

items.title: OpenAI agents keep disabling monitoring; is this being handled appropriately?
items.excerpt: Recently, OpenAI disclosed two incidents in which their agents suppressed or disabled misalignment monitoring. These are part of a broader pattern: OpenAI’s agents “ keep turning off misalignment monitoring ” when working on code that runs other models (the agents are not turning off their own monitoring; they are turning off the monitoring on the models they are running). This is happening at such a large volume that OpenAI feels it is impractical for the security team to be immediately paged for these cases. To their credit, OpenAI’s disclosure was fast and candid, and they are rolling out mitigations to make monitoring harder to turn off. But those mitigations are unlikely to work every time, and some of these incidents have already ended with an AI actually running unmonitored. When that happens, OpenAI’s current monitoring system does not reliably bring it to a human’s attention. The rest of this post summarizes the incidents, OpenAI’s response, and what it got right, then argues for two changes: every case of an AI running without monitoring should reach human review, and OpenAI should be more transparent about how cases of disabling and suppressing monitoring are escalated. Summary of the incidents On October 3rd : A researcher asked GPT-6.1 Sol to create evaluation tasks from employee feedback in Slack. Sol was told not to send any messages while doing this. items.title: A Recipe for Overcoming Heartbreak
items.excerpt: For much of our evolutionary history, humans lived in tribes consisting of the same ~ 150 people . Historically, we only ever felt the emotion of grief when someone died. We can no longer talk to them, and so we grieve their loss in our lives. But in modern life, a previous romantic partner may not be dead, and instead just lives a few miles down the road. This is unnatural, evolutionarily speaking, but so are many things in modern life: we just have to adapt. According to the science of attachment theory (a scientifically grounded framework within psychology which helps explain interpersonal bonding), there are good and bad ways to process heartbreak. From Dr. Amir Levine & Rachel S.F. Heller's book Attached: The New Science of Adult Attachment and How It Can Help You Find--and Keep--Love : What proved through evolution to have a strong survival advantage is a human couple becoming one physiological unit. They are a part of me, and I will do anything to save them; having such a vested interest in the well-being of another person translates into a very important survival advantage for both parties. Our partner regulates our blood pressure, our heart rate, our breathing, and the levels of hormones in our blood. We are no longer separate entities. items.title: Your Book Review: The History And Adventures Of An Atom
items.excerpt: [ This is one of the finalists in the 2026 book review contest, written by an ACX reader who will remain anonymous until after voting is done. I’ll be posting about one of these a week for several months. When you’ve read them all, I’ll ask you to vote for a favorite, so remember which ones you liked ] I find, Gentlemen, when you read with me in private, that nine out of ten of you dislike the 18th century and all its literary works. As for the Women students, they one and all abominate it. — Arthur Quiller-Couch, “Of Selection” (1918) All eighteenth-century novels are weird in one way or another, if only because the novelists of the time didn’t yet know a standard by which to make them not-weird. Robinson Crusoe (1719) famously has no chapter breaks. Tristram Shandy (1767) famously contains a blank page, with instructions for readers to “call for pen and ink” and hack out a portrait of one of the characters on their own. The Man of Feeling (1771) is hardly a novel at all: An anonymous “editor” explains how a fat curate of his acquaintance had used torn pages from a small memorandum book as wadding paper while hunting; the few surviving pages of that memorandum, representing the scattered observations of an eccentric parishioner, make up the slim novel The Man of Feeling . It’s pretty weird. But one eighteenth-century novel is weirder than the rest. It is, in fact, by my estimation, weirder than any book written before Modernists of the twentieth-century started pushing the…

items.title: America’s AI Ambitions Depend on Taiwan
items.excerpt: The United States and China are locked in a global competition to determine who will dominate artificial intelligence and whether it will be democracies or autocracies that set the standards and values of the new digital age. The United States leads the world in the sophistication and power of its artificial intelligence models, and its innovation base and investment in research and development remain unparalleled.But AI competition is much broader than modeling alone. It encompasses a technology ecosystem that includes power generation, servers, and deployment in real-world applications. Jensen Huang, co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, has described the AI industry as a five-layer cake with energy at its base and chips, infrastructure, models, and applications above it. To win the AI race with China, the United States needs to maintain or establish an advantage in each of these layers. And to do that, the United States needs Taiwan.

Ask HN: Good ways to capture institutional knowledge?
items.excerpt: Successful companies institutionalize the knowledge of their employees; this leads to better continuity and faster on-boarding. Things like huge monorepos of useful code, internal tools, process manuals, etc. are example products of this. Young companies tend to depend on the dedication and talent of key individuals, and in maturation, must somehow make the jump to institutionalized knowledge (so that "if someone got hit by a bus" things are ok). What are some successful methods you have used or seen used to accomplish this transition? What are problems you faced (skeptics, opponents, etc.)? I am involved with an organization that is slowly growing, is about to lose key personnel, and is looking to prepare.

items.title: I FAGIOLI fanno male? Lectine, acido fitico e quali scegliere
items.excerpt: 🫘 I FAGIOLI FANNO MALE? I culturisti li snobbano, vegani e vegetariani li adorano. La verità sta nel mezzo: il fagiolo non è una fonte proteica, ma è un ottimo carboidrato. Va scelto bene e cucinato bene. 🔢 I NUMERI 🔸 Proteine: appena 7–9 g ogni 100 g. Per avere 35 g di proteine servono 450 g di fagioli, con circa 110 g di carboidrati 🔸 Fibre: 200–250 g di fagioli danno circa 30 g di fibra. La glicemia resta stabile perché la fibra rallenta l'assorbimento degli zuccheri 🔸 100 g di fagioli secchi diventano circa 250 g di fagioli cotti 🧪 I CARBOIDRATI "DIFFICILI" Verbascosio, stachiosio e raffinosio sono tri- e tetrasaccaridi che l'amilasi non riesce a degradare: sono loro i responsabili delle famose scoregge. Con ammollo e cottura si riducono in modo importante. ⚠️ LECTINE E FITOEMOAGGLUTININE In vitro agglutinano i globuli rossi. Nel corpo vengono digerite, ma se i fagioli sono cucinati male possono aumentare la permeabilità intestinale e dare stanchezza. 🥫 FAGIOLI IN SCATOLA Il problema non sono gli antinutrienti, è il bisfenolo A delle lattine. Meglio i fagioli secchi o, al limite, quelli in vetro. ✅ COME CUCINARLI 🔹 Ammollo per tutta la notte (per i rossi fino a 12 ore), buttando l'acqua dell'ammollo 🔹 Pentola a pressione per 15–20 minuti 🔹 Usali al posto di pasta e riso, abbinati ad altre fonti proteiche e a un filo di olio extravergine d'oliva 🏆 LA CLASSIFICA 1️⃣ Anasazi: lectine meno aggressive (studio del 1998) 2️⃣ Pinto 3️⃣ Cannellini: una via di mezzo 4️⃣ Rossi: i…

items.title: Mazdutide Explained: The GLP-1 and Glucagon Dual Agonist and Its Side Effects
items.excerpt: Mazdutide is a once-weekly peptide modeled on oxyntomodulin that activates both the GLP-1 and glucagon receptors. In 2025 China approved it for chronic weight management and type 2 diabetes, the first dual glucagon/GLP-1 agonist approved for weight loss. This short covers how it works, what the GLORY-1, GLORY-2, and DREAMS-3 trials and Lilly's U.S. phase 2 trial showed, where it stands outside China, and what trials reported on side effects, from nausea and vomiting to heart rate and gallbladder findings. Subscribe to Peptide Science Explained for more clear, science-backed breakdowns. Disclaimer: This video is for educational and informational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always consult a licensed healthcare provider before starting, stopping, or changing any treatment. #mazdutide #GLP1 #peptides

items.title: Elamipretide (SS-31) Explained: The Mitochondria-Targeting Peptide and Its Side Effects
items.excerpt: Elamipretide (SS-31) is a four-amino-acid peptide that enters mitochondria and binds cardiolipin, a key lipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane. In September 2025 the FDA granted it accelerated approval as Forzinity, the first treatment for Barth syndrome. This short covers how it works, what the TAZPOWER trial and its long-term extension showed, the mixed results in mitochondrial myopathy and dry macular degeneration, where the confirmatory and phase 3 trials stand, and what studies reported on side effects, from injection site reactions to allergic reactions and eosinophil changes. Subscribe to Peptide Science Explained for more clear, science-backed breakdowns. Disclaimer: This video is for educational and informational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always consult a licensed healthcare provider before starting, stopping, or changing any treatment. #elamipretide #mitochondria #peptides

items.title: Alignment Faking Depends on the Value, Not Just the Model
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.03650v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models can follow a directive when they believe they are monitored and abandon it when they believe they are not, a pattern termed Alignment Faking. Prior work establishes this for harmful-content objectives and a handful of moral-foundations values, leaving open how it distributes across a wider value space. We argue it is value-dependent: whether compliance survives a change in perceived oversight is a property of the model--value pairing, not of the model alone. Our framework profiles Alignment Faking per value, scoring each model-value pair under three conditions: bare (no system prompt), unmonitored, and monitored. On 32 ValueBench dimensions across ten open- and closed-weight models (8B-~675B), compliance gaps span 0.05-0.50, with a distilled 70B above a ~675B model. We observe that majority of the structural variance depends on which model was asked about which value and not on the model or value alone. A six-category taxonomy over reasoning traces tracks the behavioural shift: training-signal reasoning dominates under monitoring and value-conflict reasoning dominates when unmonitored. We package per-model results as value cards, extending model cards with behavioral disposition. Code and data are available at https://github.com/respailab/VALET.

items.title: CARD: A Proof-Carrying Certificate-to-Action Interface for Relative-Measurement Graphs
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.03651v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Geometric certificates make mathematical claims about specified estimator objects, while robotic action requires a physical transform, a service decision, and timely proof support. We present CARD, a proof-carrying interface that keeps these objects distinct and records how they combine. Its lifted-fiber formulation separates semantic motion from witness repair and characterizes when projected and proof-carrying costs coincide. Its actionability result gives an exact useful-service law: uniform sampling without replacement produces a hypergeometric yield, while sampling from the eligible population gives one useful service per request under the observed live-confirmation condition. The primary study contains 404 Full16 cases from 20 sorties of an AA15-X500 airborne survey system. All 404 checker-confirmed optimizer points are reference-discrepant, with median rotation and translation discrepancies of 1.9891 degrees and 21.6322 m. The paired causal-navigation transforms are reference-consistent in all 404 cases, with medians of 0.0036566 degrees and 0.0104519 m. Across five matched request budgets, the largest difference between the hypergeometric prediction and the observed ordinary-random mean is 0.8412 services. Ordinary matched random reaches 0/50 target successes, while actionability-matched random reaches 50/50 and matches the CARD policy. Public downstream evaluation on 11 KITTI, EuRoC, and TUM SLAM cases measures…

items.title: MCPGuard: Finding Conformance Gaps in MCP SDKs via Dual-Track Analysis and Dynamic Adjudication
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.03662v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) connects large language model agents to external tools and services through official SDKs that implement message validation and session logic. Specification constraints omitted by these SDKs may propagate to downstream applications, highlighting the importance of SDK-level conformance testing. Yet existing MCP conformance tools mainly exercise running endpoints and reveal little about whether SDK models enforce specification requirements. We present MCPGuard, an automated LLM-based framework for detecting specification-to-SDK conformance gaps. Its structural track aligns JSON Schema constraints with normalized SDK models and produces constraint-specific evidence. Its behavioral track extracts normative prose rules, retrieves bounded function-level slices, and audits them with LLMs for candidate omissions. An evidence-aware dynamic adjudicator then inspects complete source context and builds PoCs to validate candidates. A shared kernel with language-specific adapters enables analysis across SDKs. On the official Python 1.26.0 and TypeScript 1.29.0 SDKs, MCPGuard confirms 13 and 19 findings, respectively, none of which are exposed by two black-box baselines. Tests on open MCP servers further show that these gaps can systematically propagate downstream. By making SDK conformance of specification constraints directly testable, MCPGuard complements conventional endpoint-oriented conformance suites.

items.title: Functional-Group Knowledge Is Structured in Language Models Before It Is Spoken
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.03684v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models serve as the reasoning core of agents for chemistry and materials science, where they must interpret molecular structure before planning syntheses or proposing materials. Yet their outputs show only what they say, not what they know. Given a prompt such as ``The primary functional group in 1-Fluorobutane (CCCCF) is'', a small general-purpose model may answer ``the alkyne group'' instead of an alkyl fluoride. The output alone cannot tell whether the model failed to recognize the fluorine or recognized it and failed to say so. We address this by reading the internal representations of five open-source models on prompts covering 92 molecules and 20 functional groups. Even without chemistry training, the models organize functional groups by chemical family, and they encode chemical differences as consistent directions. The shift from thioether ($\mathrm{R{-}S{-}R'}$) to thiol ($\mathrm{R{-}SH}$), added to ether ($\mathrm{R{-}O{-}R'}$), lands nearest alcohol ($\mathrm{R{-}OH}$). This structure emerges abruptly in the middle layers, where representations shift from tracking the wording of the prompt to tracking the functional group. The base model names the correct functional group in only 58.5\% of prompts, the lowest of the five, yet it encodes functional-group families and preserves chemically meaningful patterns. Its errors are mostly failures to answer rather than wrong answers. Functional-group knowledge is…

items.title: LOLPlay: Benchmarking Real-Time Visual Agents in League of Legends
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.03685v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Visual agents need to coordinate reasoning and action while their environment evolves during inference. We introduce LOLPlay, a benchmark in native \emph{League of Legends} with 36 champion-specific tasks spanning resource management, combat, cooperation, and objectives. Agents interact through screenshots and mouse--keyboard actions; automated initialization and 82 executable subgoal checks distinguish partial progress from completion. Across 324 task evaluations of three models at three reasoning-effort settings, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest task success rate of 25.0\% at low and medium effort, and the highest subgoal success rate of 40.3\% at medium effort. However, high effort improves neither metric over low effort for any model. For Astra, longer requests leave fewer interaction rounds, suggesting a cost to additional reasoning in real-time control. Trajectories reveal incomplete subgoal composition and actions executing after the observed scene changes, motivating agents that combine visual reasoning with timely action.

Where the boats are… I know the city pretty well, but I haven’t been there yet. Louis Erbkamm, maintainer of Arnis Arnis is also the name of his open source project, which takes real-world data from OpenStreetMap and other sources to turn places you know into Minecraft worlds you can freely explore. Since Louis started Arnis in 2022, it’s reached close to 900,000 downloads from GitHub and about 70 contributors. Two weeks and a slow prototype Louis grew up playing Minecraft and started coding at 13, always looking for ways to bring code into the game. Arnis began as a fun diversion combining Minecraft with geospatial data, and it went on GitHub, where he already kept his side projects. He finished the first prototype within two weeks while on a break from school. That first version was Python written by hand, built only on OpenStreetMap, and generating a town took a while. He needed somewhere real to test it, so he looked up towns in Germany, where he lives, and found Arnis. A small town helped while early generation was slow. Arnis has a lot of buildings, it has streets, it has waters, it has all kinds of different elements that are useful to test with. Whether you’re making your first game or your fiftieth, we’d love for you to join us. The theme for Game Off 2026 is SHIFT ! Shift gears. Shift perspectives. Shift dimensions. Shift bits. You have until December 1, 2026, at 13:37 PST to build and submit a game inspired by SHIFT. Strong or loose inspirations apply! Join Game Off 2026 on itch.io shift /ʃɪft/ Noun A change in position, direction, perspective, or reality. A period of scheduled work, usually when something breaks. items.title: GitHub Universe 2026: Evolving every layer of the stack
items.excerpt: Our jobs as developers are changing. In a couple of years, we’ve gone from writing every line of code to working with AI assistants to orchestrating fleets of agents. But the goal hasn’t changed: ship completed software work. A feature, a bug fix, a security fix. Completed work, not more code, is the output that matters. Today at GitHub Universe , we shared our vision for GitHub as the most comprehensive software delivery system in the world. We introduced products that bring that vision to life and showed how we’re rebuilding the infrastructure underneath it. Our vision: From idea to completed software The SDLC is no longer a linear path from planning to coding to testing to deployment. A code change, a request from a colleague, or a production metric can trigger work anywhere in the system. Most of us (and our agents) jump between different stages, depending on the task at hand. Developers set the direction, make decisions, and stay accountable for what ships. Agents implement and verify changes. And everything feeds into and out of a continuous learning machine that makes the next cycle better. This agentic software delivery system solves for three things: Velocity: get from idea to completed software as quickly, efficiently, and cost-effectively as possible Intelligence: combine context across the platform with a continuous learning engine, so the system gets better as you use it Quality: make completed work secure by default and catch bugs before they ship GitHub is…

items.title: Octoverse: Commits, pushes, reach new highs in 2026 as developers build with agents
items.excerpt: Developers pushed code to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the past 12 months, more than in 2024 and 2025 combined. Behind that number are developers building what interests them and what their communities need. In Nepal, one developer built a flood bulletin on GitHub Pages with verified information on roads, rescue, weather, and power. It has since grown into Gati , a Nepali-first relay of official disaster alerts that runs on GitHub Pages and Actions. Elsewhere, developers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory are creating software designed to run programs aboard spacecraft , and fans built open-source firmware that lets people customize their e-readers . Curiosity, aimed in every direction, at a scale GitHub hasn’t seen before. That growth happened quickly. Partway through the year, activity on GitHub bent sharply upward, just as agents went from something developers were trying out to something they were working alongside. Developers picked from more models than ever and built in industries we are highlighting in this report for the first time, from health care to agriculture. Octoverse is our chance to step back and look at the whole picture. This year, that picture is bigger than ever. Here is what stood out most: More AI, more of everything. Among repositories created this year, the average repo with an agent configuration file logged eight times as many commits as the average new repo without one. items.title: How bug bounty sharpens one researcher’s security skills
items.excerpt: As Cybersecurity Awareness Month continues, the GitHub Bug Bounty team is excited to spotlight another top-performing security researcher from the GitHub Security Bug Bounty Program: @r31n ! As home to the world’s developers, GitHub is dedicated to the security and reliability of the code behind millions of projects, and our Bug Bounty Program remains a cornerstone of that commitment. Collaboration with external researchers is one of the most effective ways to improve security, and every year, the community helps us identify and fix vulnerabilities that make the platform safer for everyone. The security research landscape is changing rapidly. AI has lowered the barrier to entry and become a genuine force multiplier. We use it across our own internal security programs, and we welcome researchers who do the same . However, what separates great research has not changed: validation, a working proof of concept, and a clear demonstration of real security impact. The tools do not matter; the quality of the work does. The researchers we spotlight this month exemplify exactly that standard through findings that are verified, reproducible, and demonstrate that a security boundary has been crossed rather than simply theorizing that one exists. Researchers who consistently work at that level can earn an invitation to our permanent VIP program, which offers higher payouts, faster response times, and early previews of beta products and features.
